pos: n. (one of the seven chamberlains of Ahasuerus; named once)
etymology: A Persian name of uncertain sense, commonly explained as happy or God-given; one of the seven eunuchs who served in the royal presence, Esther 1:10.
biblical_def: Abagtha is named once, in the roll of the seven officers sent to fetch the queen: “On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king” (Esther 1:10). The Authorized Version's chamberlain renders a word for a eunuch, and the margin at that verse notes it. The errand they were given was shameful: “To bring Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to shew the people and the princes her beauty: for she was fair to look on” (Esther 1:11). She would not come: “But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king's commandment by his chamberlains: therefore was the king very wroth, and his anger burned in him” (Esther 1:12). The refusal set the whole book in motion, for the council's remedy opened the throne: “let the king give her royal estate unto another that is better than she” (Esther 1:19). Abagtha is one of seven men named and then never mentioned again, which is itself worth noticing. The Holy Ghost records the names of the servants who carried a drunken king's message, because the book of Esther is written to show that nothing in that palace, down to the errand-boys, lay outside the hand that was preparing a deliverance.

corruption_summary: Vashti's refusal is made a charter for throwing off the order of the home, where the chapter condemns a husband who used his wife as a spectacle.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther 1 is routinely preached as the first chapter of liberation: Vashti stands as the woman who said no, and the complementarian order of Scripture is held to be answered by her. The text does not grant it. What is rebuked in the chapter is Ahasuerus — a king drunk on the seventh day of his own feast, sending seven eunuchs to parade his wife's body before a hall of princes. A husband's headship is given for the protection and honour of his wife, and a man who turns it to her shame has abandoned the office, not exercised it. That Vashti would not be displayed is not a case against the order; it is a case against this man.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the decree which followed — “that every man should bear rule in his own house” (Esther 1:22) — was a heathen council's attempt to legislate what God had already established and what the king had just betrayed. Authority in the home is not secured by edict; it is exercised in self-denying love or it is forfeited.

pos: n. (one of the seven princes of Persia and Media; named once)
etymology: A Persian name, variously explained as unconquered or as a testimony; one of the seven counsellors who saw the king's face, Esther 1:14.
biblical_def: Admatha is named once, among the inner council of the empire: “And the next unto him was Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom” (Esther 1:14). To see the king's face was a privilege of the highest rank, since access to the Persian presence was guarded by law, as Esther herself would afterwards discover. These were the men Ahasuerus consulted when his wife had crossed him: “Then the king said to the wise men, which knew the times, (for so was the king's manner toward all that knew law and judgment” (Esther 1:13). Their counsel was given by one of their number and was wholly political: “And Memucan answered before the king and the princes, Vashti the queen hath not done wrong to the king only, but also to all the princes, and to all the people that are in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus” (Esther 1:16). The result was an empire-wide edict: “For he sent letters into all the king's provinces, into every province according to the writing thereof, and to every people after their language, that every man should bear rule in his own house” (Esther 1:22). Admatha sat first in the kingdom and is remembered for one meeting, in which seven wise men who knew the times failed to tell a king the truth about himself.

corruption_summary: Worldly counsel is credited with wisdom because it is expert and well placed; Esther 1 shows seven of the ablest men in the world counselling a king badly.
corruption_paragraphs: These were the wise men “which knew the times” (Esther 1:13) — the phrase describes exactly what our own age prizes: men who read the moment, who know law and judgment, who sit at the centre. Scripture is content to grant their competence and then to show the fruit of it. Not one of them said to Ahasuerus that he was drunk, that the command had been disgraceful, or that a wife is not a spectacle. They framed the queen's refusal as a threat to public order and proposed an irreversible decree. Worldly wisdom is real, and it is not the fear of the LORD, and the difference shows under pressure.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that counsel must be measured by the word of God and not by the standing of the counsellor. Seven princes who saw the king's face gave advice that cost a queen her place and set a throne empty for a Jewish orphan, and God used their folly to do it.

pos: n. (the fifth of the ten sons of Haman; named once)
etymology: A Persian name of uncertain sense; one of the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, slain in Shushan and afterwards hanged, Esther 9:8.
biblical_def: Adalia is named once, in the bare list of Haman's sons: “And Poratha, and Adalia, and Aridatha” (Esther 9:8). The verse is three names and nothing more, and the ten names together occupy two and a half verses of a book which elsewhere lingers over banquets and decrees. The record of their end is equally plain: “The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand” (Esther 9:10). The last clause matters: the Jews of Shushan defended themselves and took nothing, so that no one could say the day had been for plunder. Esther then asked for the bodies to be exposed: “Then said Esther, If it please the king, let it be granted to the Jews which are in Shushan to do to morrow also according unto this day's decree, and let Haman's ten sons be hanged upon the gallows” (Esther 9:13). The gallows were their father's own, built for Mordecai: “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified” (Esther 7:10). Adalia's name survives for one reason, that he stood with his father in a plot to destroy a whole people, and perished in the destruction his father had designed.

corruption_summary: The death of Haman's sons is held up as vindictive excess, where Esther 9 presents a lawful defence under a decree that could not be revoked.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther 9 is the chapter most often produced to prove the Old Testament cruel, and the ten sons are the centre of the charge: children killed for their father's crime, and their corpses hung up at a queen's request. The chapter answers the charge in its own details. Haman's decree was written and sealed and, by the law of the Persians, could not be recalled; the only remedy the king could give was a second decree permitting the Jews to stand for their lives, and that is exactly what the day was. The sons were not infants but men who had their father's place and purpose. And the thrice-repeated note that the Jews “laid they not their hand” on the spoil (Esther 9:10) is the writer's proof that this was defence and not rapine.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the Psalm states: “His mischief shall return upon his own head” (Psalm 7:16). Haman built a gallows and hanged on it; he decreed a slaughter and his house fell in it. God governs the ends of the wicked by their own means, and the book of Esther, which never once names Him, is written to show it.

pos: n. (the ninth of the ten sons of Haman; named once)
etymology: A Persian name of uncertain sense, sometimes explained as the delight of Hari; one of the ten sons of Haman, Esther 9:9.
biblical_def: Aridai is named once, in a verse of four names: “And Parmashta, and Arisai, and Aridai, and Vajezatha” (Esther 9:9). He is not to be confused with Aridatha of the verse before, though the names stand close; the Authorized Version keeps them distinct as the Hebrew does. What binds the ten together is their father's design, stated without softening: “And he thought scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone; for they had shewed him the people of Mordecai: wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, even the people of Mordecai” (Esther 3:6). It was not a quarrel with a man but a plan against a nation, and it was prosecuted by letters into every province. The ten died in the defence that followed: “The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand” (Esther 9:10). The king granted Esther's further petition at once: “And the king commanded it so to be done: and the decree was given at Shushan; and they hanged Haman's ten sons” (Esther 9:14). A name recorded once, in a list, belonging to a man whose only act in Scripture was to inherit his father's hatred.

corruption_summary: Haman's plot is reduced to a personal feud, where Esther 3 names it as an attempt to destroy a whole people and the Scripture treats it as warfare against the seed.
corruption_paragraphs: A common handling of Esther makes the conflict a court rivalry: a proud official slighted by a stubborn Jew, with the rest escalation. Esther 3:6 forbids that reading. Haman thought it beneath him to touch Mordecai alone, and so determined to destroy “all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.” The object was the people, because of the people's God and the promise carried in them. That is the same enmity Scripture traces from Pharaoh's midwives to Herod's soldiers, and it is not explained by wounded pride.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence that governs a book in which God is never named. A sleepless night, a forgotten chronicle, a casual question about who should be honoured, and the whole machinery of the empire turns. Aridai and his brethren are a line in the record of what came of fighting against the people of promise.

pos: n. (the eighth of the ten sons of Haman; named once)
etymology: A Persian name of uncertain sense; one of the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, named in the list at Esther 9:9.
biblical_def: Arisai is named once: “And Parmashta, and Arisai, and Aridai, and Vajezatha” (Esther 9:9). The ten names are given in full because the king asked for an account and was given one. He had heard the number already: “And the king said unto Esther the queen, The Jews have slain and destroyed five hundred men in Shushan the palace, and the ten sons of Haman; what have they done in the rest of the king's provinces? now what is thy petition?” (Esther 9:12). The verdict of the whole affair is set down afterwards in a single sentence that reads like a proverb: “But when Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked device, which he devised against the Jews, should return upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows” (Esther 9:25). Scripture had said it long before: “His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate” (Psalm 7:16). Arisai is one of ten men whose names are preserved only as part of a device that recoiled. There is no biography to give; the point of the list is the completeness of the reversal, and the Holy Ghost counted the sons out one by one to make it plain.

corruption_summary: Lists of unknown names are dismissed as filler, where the ten sons are counted out to show a wicked device returning exactly upon its author.
corruption_paragraphs: Genealogies and name-lists are the parts of Scripture modern readers skip and modern critics call accretion. Esther 9 shows what a list can do. Haman had cast lots to fix a day for the extermination of a people and had got a sealed decree for it; the chapter answers with a precise inventory of what became of his own house, name by name, so that the symmetry cannot be missed. The device “should return upon his own head” (Esther 9:25), and the ten names are the measure of how far it returned.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's justice is exact and not approximate. He does not merely frustrate the wicked; He turns the instrument in their hand. Haman's gallows, Haman's decree, Haman's chosen month — each became the means of the deliverance he had set out to prevent.

pos: n. pl. (one of the peoples who wrote to Artaxerxes against the building of Jerusalem; named once)
etymology: A gentilic plural, commonly understood as the men of Erech in Babylonia (Genesis 10:10); one of the colonist peoples listed at Ezra 4:9.
biblical_def: The Archevites are named once, in the roll of those who joined the letter against Jerusalem: “Then wrote Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions; the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites” (Ezra 4:9). These were the transplanted peoples settled in the land by the Assyrian kings, and the length of the list is part of the argument: the opposition was broad, official, and literate. Their charge was framed to touch an emperor where he would feel it: “Be it known unto the king, that the Jews which came up from thee to us are come unto Jerusalem, building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls thereof, and joined the foundations” (Ezra 4:12). It worked for a season: “Now when the copy of king Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went up in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power” (Ezra 4:23). But the work was not finally stopped: “And the elders of the Jews builded, and they prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. And they builded, and finished it, according to the commandment of the God of Israel” (Ezra 6:14).

corruption_summary: The opposition in Ezra 4 is described as a dispute between rival communities, where the text presents a concerted attempt to stop the house of God by law.
corruption_paragraphs: It is usual to read Ezra 4 as a neighbourhood conflict: settled peoples resenting returning exiles, with both sides equally partisan. The chapter is written from a different angle. The letter accuses Jerusalem of being “the rebellious and the bad city” (Ezra 4:12) and asks the crown to search the records; the aim is not coexistence but cessation, and it is pursued through the proper channels of a legitimate empire. Opposition to the work of God is frequently lawful, literate and well documented, and that does not make it less opposition.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the house was finished through preaching. The decree stopped the stones; Haggai and Zechariah started them again, and Ezra 6:14 attributes the completion to the prophesying of the two prophets and to the commandment of the God of Israel, with the Persian kings' decrees mentioned afterwards. The order of that sentence is the doctrine.

pos: n. (a people in league with Egypt, named once in Ezekiel's burden)
etymology: Hebrew Kub, a people of uncertain location, named with Ethiopia, Libya and Lydia among Egypt's confederates; Ezekiel 30:5.
biblical_def: Chub is named once, in the list of nations appointed to fall with Egypt: “Ethiopia, and Libya, and Lydia, and all the mingled people, and Chub, and the men of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword” (Ezekiel 30:5). Where Chub lay Scripture does not say, and the dictionary will not supply what revelation withholds; the company it keeps places it among the African and Asiatic peoples who served in Pharaoh's armies. The burden around it is unmistakable: “And the sword shall come upon Egypt, and great pain shall be in Ethiopia, when the slain shall fall in Egypt, and they shall take away her multitude, and her foundations shall be broken down” (Ezekiel 30:4). The reason the allies fall with her is given next: “Thus saith the LORD; They also that uphold Egypt shall fall; and the pride of her power shall come down” (Ezekiel 30:6). To uphold Egypt is to stand where Egypt stands, and Egypt's place was already fixed. Isaiah had put the lesson to Judah in the form of a woe: “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD!” (Isaiah 31:1). Chub is a name on the losing side of that sentence.

corruption_summary: An unlocated name is taken as evidence of a confused text; the honest course is to say that Scripture names Chub and does not place it.
corruption_paragraphs: Chub is a standing example of a word that invites two kinds of overreach. Critical treatments use the uncertainty to argue for a corrupt or conjectural text and propose emendations; devotional treatments invent a geography and state it with confidence. Both say more than is given. The Authorized Version renders the Hebrew that stands; the location is unknown; and a reference work that admits the limit is worth more than one that fills it with a guess dressed as knowledge. What is certain is the company and the verdict, and those are the point of the verse.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Isaiah pressed on Judah and Ezekiel pressed on the nations: those who uphold Egypt fall with Egypt. Alliances are not neutral. To lend strength to what God has appointed for judgment is to take a place in the judgment, whatever the treaty says.

pos: n. (a people or land whose tents Habakkuk saw in affliction; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Kushan, probably a lengthened form of Cush, set in parallel with Midian; named once, Habakkuk 3:7.
biblical_def: Cushan is named once, in the vision of Habakkuk's third chapter: “I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble” (Habakkuk 3:7). The parallel with Midian is the chief clue to the name, and the picture is of a nomad people whose tent-curtains shake as God passes by. The whole chapter is a prayer written as a march. Before this verse the earth itself gives way: “He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways are everlasting” (Habakkuk 3:6). After it the prophet asks whether the rivers and sea had offended, since the Lord came out against them with horses: “Was the LORD displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation?” (Habakkuk 3:8). The answer is that the convulsion of creation is for the saving of a people, which is why the chariots are called chariots of salvation. The prayer that opens the chapter is the key to it: “O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3:2).

corruption_summary: Habakkuk 3 is treated as borrowed storm-god poetry, where the chapter is a prophet's prayer resting on God's acts in history.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the chapter speaks of mountains scattering, rivers angered and chariots in the sea, it is regularly explained as recycled Near-Eastern storm-god imagery with a thin Israelite coat of paint. The explanation fails on the chapter's own anchors. It is not a nature-hymn but a recital of the exodus and the conquest — Teman and Paran, Midian and Cushan, the sea divided, the nations driven asunder — and its subject is named: “thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people.” Poetry that remembers real deliverances is not myth, and the figure of trembling tent-curtains is the ordinary speech of a people who lived in tents.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Habakkuk's petition, which is the sanest prayer in a dark time: revive thy work, make it known, and “in wrath remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3:2). He had been told that Babylon was coming and he did not ask for the sentence to be lifted; he asked that God would be God in the middle of it.

pos: n. (the father of the Babylonian king who sent letters to Hezekiah; named twice)
etymology: Babylonian in origin, the element -adan appearing in royal names of that house; known in Scripture only as the father of Berodach-baladan, 2 Kings 20:12 and Isaiah 39:1.
biblical_def: Baladan is named twice, and only ever as a father: “At that time Berodachbaladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present unto Hezekiah: for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick” (2 Kings 20:12). Isaiah records the same embassy and spells the son's name a little differently: “At that time Merodachbaladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: for he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered” (Isaiah 39:1). The embassy was courteous and it was the occasion of Hezekiah's worst hour: “And Hezekiah hearkened unto them, and shewed them all the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not” (2 Kings 20:13). The sentence came at once from Isaiah: “Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store unto this day, shall be carried into Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD” (2 Kings 20:17). The man who had prayed through a siege and through a death-sentence was undone by flattery from the east, and the house he displayed was the house that went into captivity.

corruption_summary: The two spellings of the son's name are produced as a contradiction, and Hezekiah's fault is softened to a lapse of discretion rather than pride of heart.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors attach to this episode. The first makes much of Berodach- against Merodach-, as though the Authorized Version had preserved an error; but variant forms of a foreign royal name are ordinary in Hebrew as in English, the initial letters are close in the script, and the translators rendered faithfully what each book has. The second softens the sin. Hezekiah is said to have been merely indiscreet with state secrets, a diplomatic blunder. Chronicles names the thing itself: his heart was lifted up, and he rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how pride finds its door. Hezekiah stood firm under Sennacherib's army and under his own death-sentence, and fell to a courtesy visit from a distant king who had heard he was sick. Deliverance is a more dangerous hour than danger, and the treasures a man has just been given are the likeliest things to be shown off and then carried away.

pos: n. (father of Elidad, the prince of Benjamin who divided the land; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Kislon, hope or confidence, from a root meaning to be firm or to trust; named once, Numbers 34:21.
biblical_def: Chislon is named once, in the shortest possible form: “Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chislon” (Numbers 34:21). The verse belongs to a commission given before the land was entered. Two men were named to lead the division: “These are the names of the men which shall divide the land unto you: Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun” (Numbers 34:17), and then a representative from each tribe was added: “And ye shall take one prince of every tribe, to divide the land by inheritance” (Numbers 34:18). Chislon's son Elidad was Benjamin's man on that commission. The chapter closes by grounding the whole arrangement in a command: “These are they whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance unto the children of Israel in the land of Canaan” (Numbers 34:29). The point of the list is that the inheritance was not to be settled by the strong taking what they could hold. Priest and captain stood at the head, a prince of every tribe stood with them, the boundaries had been described beforehand, and the lot was the LORD's. Chislon's name, which means confidence, is preserved for one reason: his son was trusted with other men's portions.

corruption_summary: The division of Canaan is described as conquest dressed in religious language, where Numbers 34 shows a commission, fixed borders and a command given before a foot was set in the land.
corruption_paragraphs: The settlement of Canaan is commonly presented as a land-grab retold with God's name attached. Numbers 34 is a difficult chapter for that account. The borders are described in detail before the crossing; the commissioners are named before there is anything to divide; a priest and a civil leader share the headship; and one prince from every tribe is set beside them so that no tribe is apportioned without its own witness present. The chapter ends by referring the whole arrangement to the LORD's command, not to the army's success.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that lawful authority is answerable, plural and bounded. God gave the land, fixed its borders, appointed the men, and required a representative of each tribe to stand by while the lots fell. Where an inheritance is divided among brethren, that pattern is still wisdom.
